title: The Confidence Trap
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that organisations routinely promote the wrong people into leadership because they mistake confidence for competence. He opens with the data: Gartner finds only 38 percent of employees satisfied with their manager, studies put new manager failure at 40 to 60 percent within two years, and DDI reports trust in immediate managers falling from 46 to 29 percent. He explains the psychology through Dunning and Kruger and research showing that overconfident candidates win selection processes because their self-deception reads as credibility. Traditional interviews, he says, mainly identify people who are good at interviews, and most firms also promote on past functional performance rather than leadership potential. The cultural cost is that people learn certainty is rewarded over curiosity, which makes admitting uncertainty career-limiting. He recommends structured competency assessments, validated psychometrics, 360-degree input, blind shortlisting and pre-agreed rubrics, and notes that those who could fix the system are the ones it already rewarded.
points: Organisations select managers mostly on past performance in an unrelated role, which is why excellent engineers or salespeople so often struggle as leaders.
Overconfident candidates outperform more capable ones in selection because observers read their lack of visible doubt as credibility.
Rewarding confidence over competence teaches employees that certainty beats curiosity and makes admitting uncertainty career-limiting.
Structured competency-based assessment, 360-degree input and blind shortlisting reduce the charisma premium and are far more predictive than gut-feel interviews.
The leaders best placed to reform selection are those the current system already approved, which explains the inertia.
quotes: Being extraordinary at a job and being effective at managing people who do that job are related but distinct skill sets, and conflating them is one of the most reliable ways to simultaneously lose a great individual contributor and gain a mediocre leader.
We are, as a species, extraordinarily bad at distinguishing between confidence and competence and our selection processes make the problem significantly worse.
The same cognitive skills needed to perform a task well are the ones needed to recognise when you’re performing it badly.
Traditional job interviews are, the evidence suggests, remarkably good at doing one thing: identifying people who are good at interviews.
Decisiveness looks like leadership. Certainty reads as authority.
Over time, that calcifies into a culture where admitting uncertainty is career-limiting, which is precisely the culture in which the worst decisions get made.

360-degree assessment, where candidates are evaluated by peers, direct reports, and those they report to, reduces the overconfidence premium significantly. It is harder to project false certainty to people who work alongside you every day.
The most dangerous leader in any organisation is not the one who doesn’t know the answers.
